retrieval_text: A 13-year-old girl was admitted to our hospital with a history of persistent jaundice and skin itching for one month. She is the first child of a nonconsanguineous couple with no notable family history and was born healthy via normal delivery, weighing 3200 g at birth. No significant abnormalities were observed during the perinatal period. During infancy, she exhibited skin hyperkeratosis and mild limb bone abnormalities, which progressed to ichthyosis and pronounced claw-like hands and feet by the age of 6 years. Additionally, she experienced progressive itching and recurrent desquamation of the hands and feet since the age of 6. One month prior to admission, she sought medical attention at a local hospital due to worsening jaundice and severe skin itching. At the local hospital, she was found to have acute liver failure, cholestasis, hypoalbuminemia, and abnormal blood coagulation. She received various treatments, including hepatoprotective therapy, plasma exchange, albumin infusion, and methylprednisolone pulse therapy. Following these treatments, her liver function, hypoalbuminemia, and blood coagulation improved, but jaundice and skin itching persisted. The patient was then discharged after blood samples were taken for further genetic analysis.

An eight-year-old male patient from Morocco was referred for a medical genetics consultation due to the presence of distinctive facial features and multiple physical anomalies. He was born to a healthy consanguineous couple, with the mother aged 27 and the father aged 40. There is a family history of a sister who passed away at the age of three with similar symptoms. The pregnancy was not monitored medically but was reported to be uncomplicated. At birth, the patient weighed 2800g, measured 52cm in length, and had a head circumference of 36cm. His development appeared normal during the first month of life. At eight years old, clinical examination revealed delayed growth with a weight of 15kg (–3 standard deviation), height of 80cm (–4 standard deviation), and an Occipital Frontal Circumference of 52cm (mean). The patient exhibited joint contractures, painful diffusely thickened skin, hyperpigmentation over joints, papular and/or nodular skin lesions, and gingival hypertrophy. His cognitive development was reported to be normal.

A 27-year-old male of Arabic descent visited the dermatology clinic with concerns about bilateral, symmetrical, hyperpigmented patches on his upper back. These patches had been present since birth, gradually increasing in size and darkening over the years, and were accompanied by the development of sparse hair on the affected areas. The patient reported no factors that relieved or worsened the condition, and there were no symptoms such as pain, itching, bleeding, or ulceration. A comprehensive review of systems, as well as the patient's medical, surgical, drug, and allergy history, revealed no abnormalities. There was no family history of skin diseases or other medical or congenital conditions, and the patient's four siblings had no similar complaints or skin issues. The patient's antenatal history included a normal vaginal delivery without complications, full-term birth, and up-to-date immunizations. The mother was healthy and did not take any medications during pregnancy. Examination of the body, hair, nails, and mucous membranes showed no abnormalities. The patient had not previously sought treatment for the lesions. On local skin examination, the hyperpigmented patches were found to be bilaterally symmetrical on the upper back, with the right patch measuring 15 × 7 cm and the left patch measuring 17 × 9 cm. Both patches were homogeneous and brown with irregular borders and blotchy hyperpigmented macules, and they were associated with sparse hair growth. The skin texture of the patches was similar to that of normal skin.

A 12-year-old male from an Indian family of Dravidian origin exhibited progressive hair thinning over the past 2 years. He was born at term from a consanguineous marriage with sparse hair on the scalp, eyebrows, and eyelashes. Over time, his hair regrew as coarse and curly, but he experienced increased hair loss in the last 2 years. His natal and perinatal history were unremarkable, and his developmental milestones were achieved normally. There were no issues with sweating, and both personal and family medical histories were noncontributory. No systemic involvement was noted. On general physical examination, his vital signs were normal. The anterior hairline was receded and high. The scalp hair was coarse, dry, and wiry, standing out from the head. There was sparse hair with partial alopecia on the vertex, parietal, and occipital regions, resembling androgenetic alopecia. Eyebrows, eyelashes, and body hair were sparse. Examination of the palms, soles, and oral mucosa showed no abnormalities. Nails and teeth were normal, and systemic examination revealed no abnormalities.

A 19-month-old boy, born in March 2015, presented with multiple brown-black skin pigmentations on the face, trunk, and right leg, along with several smaller satellite lesions. He was brought to the hospital due to repeated vomiting over a period of 4 days. Physical examination revealed a round face, full cheeks, prominent forehead, widely spaced eyes, fullness around the eyes, a short nose, and an everted lower lip. The largest pigmented area was on the leg, measuring approximately 13 cm in diameter with additional measurements of (13 × 10), (8 × 6), and (4 × 2) cm.
A 57-year-old Japanese woman presented with a 1-year history of a solitary erythematous plaque on the left leg.

A 28-day-old female infant, the first child of non-consanguineous parents, was admitted to our hospital due to muscle weakness, neonatal seizures, and elevated serum very long-chain fatty acids (VLCFAs) levels on March 19, 2018. She was delivered vaginally at 38 weeks and 2 days of gestation, with a birth weight of 2.21 kg. At birth, she presented with generalized muscle weakness and feeding difficulties, and experienced a seizure with low oxygen saturation one day post-birth. Despite normal results from her newborn screening, including tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS), further metabolic evaluation for neonatal seizures showed elevated VLCFA levels: C26:0 was 11.47 μmol/L (normal range < 1.31 μmol/L); C24:0/C22:0 ratio was 2.21 (normal range < 1.39), and C26:0/C22:0 ratio was 0.5 (normal range < 0.023). Phytanic and pristanic acid levels were undetectable at 15 days of age. Physical examination revealed a high forehead, large anterior fontanel, midfacial underdevelopment, high-arched palate, low-set ears, and clubfoot.

A 31-year-old male with end-stage renal disease due to chronic glomerulonephritis (IgA nephropathy) underwent a kidney transplant in December 2010 from a 25-year-old male donor who had experienced cardiac death following craniocerebral trauma. The patient had been on hemodialysis for one year before the transplant and had a history of tuberculosis contact and digestive tract hemorrhage.

A 12-year-old Arab boy presented with multiple exfoliated teeth. His oral hygiene was relatively better with gingival enlargement around erupting teeth. Most of his permanent anterior teeth were lost with severe bone destruction around his remaining teeth. His lower molars appeared floating without any bone support. There was severe palmar plantar keratosis with keratinization of the dorsal surface of his hands.

A 40-year-old, HIV-positive female presented with a 1-month history of an annular truncal eruption. She had been on highly active antiretroviral therapy (ART) for 1 year (efavirenz, lamivudine, and tenofovir) without trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis and had a CD4 count of 316 cells/mm3. Her rapid plasma reagin and Treponema pallidum hemagglutination assay were negative. The patient was commenced on oral steroids at 0.5 mg/kg and her ART was discontinued for a 2-week period. During this time her rash improved markedly and the prednisone was slowly tapered, but the rash recurred despite discontinuation of her ART.

A 21-year-old male with a recent history of gym membership and weightlifting presented to the emergency department with a 3-day history of pain and swelling in the right upper limb. His past medical history includes COVID-19 infection 12 months ago, with no family history of thromboembolic conditions. Physical examination showed a swollen and erythematous right upper limb, with palpable peripheral pulses comparable to the left side. The range of motion in the right upper limb was intact. The left upper limb and both lower limbs appeared normal. There were no signs or symptoms indicative of pulmonary embolism.

A 24-year-old male (height: 169 cm, weight: 44 kg, blood pressure: 168/75 mmHg) presented with sudden episodes of consciousness disturbance and muscle spasms. He had a history of cerebral haemorrhage, with two previous incidents occurring between the ages of 23 and 24 years. He was an only child, and his parents had no history of haemorrhage or abnormal skin conditions. A 59-year-old male presented with a history of progressive muscle weakness starting in his late twenties at the outpatient department of the rehabilitation center, Daejeon St. Mary's Hospital (Daejeon, Republic of Korea). He was born healthy at full-term and had no health issues during childhood and early adulthood, including completing mandatory national military training. In his late twenties, he experienced frequent falls and difficulty climbing stairs, with progressive muscle weakness primarily in the pelvic girdle and proximal legs, while the motor function of the upper extremities remained normal at that time. By the age of 38, he noticed muscle weakness in the upper extremities, a waddling gait, hyperlordosis of the lower back, and anterior pelvic tilt. His gait disturbance and muscle weakness continued to progress slowly. By the age of 55, he was unable to walk and required a wheelchair for mobility. His family history indicates a genetic background of autosomal recessive inheritance related to his muscle condition. One of his elder brothers exhibited similar symptoms and was diagnosed with progressive muscular dystrophy in his twenties. The patient is married to a healthy woman and has healthy children with no signs of muscle weakness.

In July 2010, a 53-year-old woman with no significant neurologic history experienced a single convulsion. Four months later, she experienced two similar convulsions, quickly progressing to status epilepticus. She was treated at an outside institution and recovered full function and returned to work.

The patient is a 55-year-old woman with a history of muscle tightening episodes for over 10 years, primarily occurring at night. She also experiences a squeezing sensation in her feet, which is worsened by wearing shoes. These symptoms have progressively worsened, leading to medical evaluation. Neurological examination showed no abnormalities in mental status, cranial nerves, muscle strength, cerebellar function, or reflexes. Sensory examination for light touch, vibration, proprioception, pin prick, and temperature was normal. Her gait, tested with shoes, was tentative, indicating foot discomfort. No trophic changes were observed in her hands or feet.

A 42-year-old female presented with sudden, widespread hair loss from the scalp occurring over a 1-day period. The patient has a history of vitiligo vulgaris and has been receiving treatment with topical tacrolimus 0.1% ointment, fluticasone ointment, and spot Narrow-band UVB (NB-UVB) phototherapy for the past 8 months. She underwent an appendicectomy 1 month ago and subsequently developed cellulitis of the left hand.

A 5-year-old male child presented with severe gingival attachment loss. The child, accompanied by parents, had no notable medical history. Over the past 2 months, the child experienced gingival bleeding and pain while chewing. Clinical oral examination showed full primary dentition, minimal plaque, moderate gingival inflammation, severe attachment loss around teeth 52, 53, 62, 63, 54, 55, 64, and 65, and a supernumerary tooth in the 51 and 61 region. Bleeding on probing was observed, and periodontal pockets around the first primary molars measured 5 mm with furcal involvement.

A 22-year-old Hispanic woman, previously in good health, experienced a severe headache (8 out of 10 on the pain scale) and blurred vision over the past 5 days. She visited the ophthalmology clinic due to a significant reduction in vision in her right eye more than her left, which gradually worsened over the 5-day period and began to interfere with her daily activities. She did not report any flashes of light or floaters in either eye. Visual acuity testing showed 20/70 in the right eye and 20/200 in the left eye. Intraocular pressures, as well as examinations of the conjunctivae, corneas, anterior chamber, and irises, were all normal. Upon dilation, the posterior chamber examination revealed optic nerve congestion and prepapilledema. There was also subretinal fluid beneath the maculae and around the optic nerves. She was referred to the hospital for further evaluation.
A 59-year-old Caucasian woman presented with progressive visual impairment in both eyes, which began in her thirties. She reported no family history of eye disorders.

The patient is a 40-year-old male who presented with memory loss. On April 9, 2019, he visited a local hospital with symptoms including tremor, involuntary urination, and incoherent speech. On April 1, 2019, he experienced disorientation while driving on a familiar road to work, resulting in a minor car accident, and he could not recall the details of the incident. These symptoms appeared 2–3 days following the accident. He reported intermittent headaches and memory loss over the past 5 years. His medical history includes being an ex-smoker with a 10 pack-year history and heavy alcohol consumption, averaging 8–10 bottles of soju per week for approximately 15 years. There is no relevant family history of brain disorders. Both the patient and his wife confirmed that there were no external circumstances outside of his workplace that could lead to poisoning from toxic substances. A review of his medical records and the history from the Korean National Health Insurance Service over the past 10 years showed no evidence of acute poisoning from toxic substances, except for exposure to CO2 arc welding at his workplace. The patient also reported experiencing difficulty breathing during welding operations due to several enclosed spaces in the workplace.
